subtopic_detail: Skin picking with specimens brought to the consultation by an older patient
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar asked to see a 67 year old woman referred from dermatology after eight months of skin picking that has left excoriations on both forearms and the upper back.

She brings a sealed container of skin flakes and lint and asks you to send it for testing, stating with complete conviction that small mites are burrowing under her skin and laying eggs. She can feel them moving, particularly at night. She has consulted four doctors and two pest controllers, has had her home fumigated twice and has thrown out her mattress. She insists she picks only to remove the organisms and would stop immediately if they were gone. Her husband has no rash and no symptoms. She is otherwise fully oriented with intact memory, has no other delusions, no hallucinations in other modalities and no formal thought disorder, and dermatology found no burrows and negative skin scrapings on two occasions.

data_table.Examination: Linear excoriations at sites reachable by her own hands with sparing of the mid upper back, no burrows, no primary lesions, orientation and memory intact, no thought disorder
data_table.Investigations: Skin scrapings for mites negative on two occasions, full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function, thyroid function and vitamin B12 within normal limits, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: A persistent delusional disorder in which the fixed false belief concerns infestation of the skin
options.rationale: An unshakeable belief in infestation held with full conviction despite two negative scrapings, an unaffected household contact and repeated professional reassurance, in a woman with otherwise intact cognition and no other psychotic features, is a monosymptomatic delusional disorder. Bringing collected specimens for analysis is close to characteristic of this presentation. (Source: RANZCP: Psychotic disorders)

options.text: Excoriation disorder in which the picking is a body focused repetitive behaviour without a fixed belief
options.rationale: In excoriation disorder the person picks at perceived skin irregularities and recognises the behaviour as their own compulsion, without a conviction that organisms are present. Her picking is secondary to a fixed belief and would stop, in her account, if the belief were resolved. (Source: RANZCP: Psychotic disorders)

options.text: A somatic symptom disorder with disproportionate health anxiety focused on an infestation of the skin
options.rationale: Somatic symptom disorder involves distressing symptoms with excessive thoughts and health anxiety, but the belief remains open to doubt and the patient can entertain alternative explanations. Complete conviction unmoved by negative testing places this beyond that threshold. (Source: RANZCP: Psychotic disorders)

options.text: An undiagnosed neurocognitive disorder presenting with a secondary psychosis and behavioural disturbance
options.rationale: Secondary psychosis in cognitive decline is an important consideration in this age group and would justify cognitive assessment and imaging. Fully intact orientation and memory with a single circumscribed delusion argues against it as the explanation. (Source: RANZCP: Psychotic disorders)

options.text: A substance induced psychotic disorder related to stimulant use presenting with tactile disturbance
options.rationale: Stimulants classically produce tactile sensations of insects on the skin and this must always be considered, but her urine drug screen is negative and the course has run for eight months without intoxication or withdrawal. The temporal pattern does not fit substance use. (Source: RANZCP: Psychotic disorders)

explanation.summary: Delusional infestation is a monosymptomatic delusional disorder in which the patient holds an unshakeable belief that they are infested by organisms, most often presenting to dermatology or general practice rather than to psychiatry. It occurs most commonly in middle aged and older women, and the presentation of collected material for analysis is so characteristic that it has its own name in the literature. The essential differential includes true infestation, which must be excluded with proper examination and scrapings, substance induced psychosis particularly with stimulants, secondary causes such as cognitive impairment, thyroid disease and vitamin B12 deficiency, and excoriation disorder in which insight is preserved. The distinction from excoriation disorder is decisive because that condition responds to behavioural therapy while delusional infestation requires an antipsychotic. Engagement is the central clinical challenge, since the patient rejects a psychiatric framing, and it is generally achieved by acknowledging the distress and the skin damage and offering treatment for those rather than by direct confrontation of the belief.
key_points: Conviction unmoved by negative testing separates delusion from health anxiety
Presenting collected specimens for analysis is close to characteristic
Exclude true infestation, stimulant use, cognitive impairment and metabolic causes
Excoriation disorder involves preserved insight and no belief in organisms
Treatment is antipsychotic medication delivered through a carefully built alliance
explanation.pearls: Note the distribution of the excoriations, because lesions confined to skin the patient can reach with sparing of the mid upper back is a strong physical sign that the lesions are self inflicted, and it can be recorded in the notes without being used to confront the patient in a way that would end the therapeutic relationship.

subtopic_detail: Recurrent winter depression in a patient who relocated to a high latitude Australian city
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 33 year old woman who moved from Cairns to Hobart four years ago for work. For the past three winters she has developed low mood, profound fatigue, sleeping ten to eleven hours a night, craving carbohydrate and gaining around 5 kg, with full remission each spring.

She has never had an episode outside the winter months and has never had a period of elevated mood, reduced need for sleep or increased goal directed activity. She describes her current episode as moderate, is working with reduced efficiency, and has no suicidal ideation and no psychotic features. Her thyroid function, full blood count, iron studies and vitamin D are normal. She is not pregnant and takes no medication. It is currently late May and she asks what will give her the best chance of getting through this winter.

data_table.Examination: Reactive but subdued affect, psychomotor activity mildly reduced, no psychotic features, cognition intact, no suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 2.0 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), haemoglobin 132 g/L (115-155), ferritin 68 micrograms/L (30-200), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 62 nmol/L (greater than 50)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Referral for cognitive behavioural therapy adapted for seasonal depression as the sole initial intervention
options.rationale: Adapted cognitive behavioural therapy performs comparably to light therapy over a single season and may reduce recurrence more in subsequent winters, making it a strong option. Availability of a trained therapist is limited and onset is slower, so it is generally combined with or follows light therapy rather than replacing it as the immediate step. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders)

options.text: Bright light therapy of adequate intensity used each morning soon after waking through the winter months
options.rationale: Recurrent depressive episodes confined to winter with hypersomnia, carbohydrate craving and weight gain, remitting each spring, is a seasonal pattern for which bright light therapy is first line and typically produces response within one to two weeks. Morning timing is what advances the delayed circadian phase thought to underlie the syndrome, and the effect is lost if the light is used in the evening. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders)

options.text: High dose colecalciferol supplementation through the winter with repeat measurement of her vitamin D level
options.rationale: Low vitamin D has been proposed as a mechanism but supplementation has not demonstrated antidepressant benefit in trials, and her level is already adequate. Correcting a value that is not deficient offers no plausible route to improvement. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders)

options.text: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor commenced now and continued as maintenance treatment year round
options.rationale: Antidepressants are effective in seasonal depression and are a legitimate option, particularly for severe episodes or when light therapy fails or is impractical. Continuous year round treatment for a condition that reliably remits each spring commits her to medication through months when she is well. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders)

options.text: Melatonin taken in the early evening to correct the circadian phase delay underlying the winter symptoms
options.rationale: Evening melatonin does advance circadian phase and has been studied in this condition, but the evidence base is far smaller than for morning bright light and it is not established as a first line treatment. It remains a reasonable adjunct in specialist hands. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Seasonal pattern is a specifier applied to recurrent major depressive episodes that begin and remit at characteristic times of year, most often with winter onset, and requires that seasonal episodes substantially outnumber non seasonal ones over a lifetime. The winter pattern is typically atypical in character, with hypersomnia, increased appetite with carbohydrate craving, weight gain and leaden fatigue, in contrast to the insomnia and anorexia of melancholic depression. Prevalence rises with latitude, which in Australia makes it more relevant in Tasmania and southern Victoria than in the tropics, and relocation to a higher latitude is a recognised trigger. Bright light therapy delivered in the morning is first line, with response usually within one to two weeks and treatment continued through the season, and adapted cognitive behavioural therapy and antidepressants are the main alternatives. Screening for bipolar disorder is essential before starting any treatment, since light therapy as well as antidepressants can precipitate a switch into mania.
key_points: Winter episodes are typically atypical with hypersomnia, overeating and weight gain
Prevalence rises with latitude, so it is more relevant in Tasmania than in the tropics
Morning timing is essential; evening light does not produce the same benefit
Bright light therapy is first line with response usually within one to two weeks
Screen for bipolarity because light therapy can precipitate a manic switch
explanation.pearls: Ask about eye disease and photosensitising medication before recommending bright light therapy, because retinal pathology and drugs such as lithium, some antipsychotics and certain antibiotics increase the risk of retinal injury, and an ophthalmological opinion is warranted before starting daily high intensity exposure.

subtopic_detail: First offence shoplifting in late middle age with personality change reported by family
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar asked to assess a 58 year old former school principal charged with shoplifting after walking out of a supermarket with items in his hands in full view of staff. He appeared unconcerned when stopped and told security he wanted the items.

His wife says that over the past two years he has become blunt to the point of rudeness with friends, laughs at things that upset others, eats sweets compulsively and has gained 11 kg, and now insists on the same meal at the same time daily. He resigned from his position after complaints about inappropriate comments. He denies any problem and attends only because his wife insisted. His memory for recent events is good, he is fully oriented, and he scores 28 out of 30 on a standard cognitive screen but cannot generate more than five animals in a minute and perseverates on a set shifting task. He describes no low mood, no elation and no reduced need for sleep.

data_table.Examination: Disinhibited and facetious in interview, no insight, orientation and recent memory intact, semantic fluency five animals in one minute, perseveration on alternating sequences, no focal neurological deficit, no parkinsonism
data_table.Investigations: Standard cognitive screen 28 out of 30, full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function, thyroid function, vitamin B12 and syphilis serology all within normal limits, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Assess for a first manic episode given the disinhibition, overspending and loss of social judgement described
options.rationale: Mania is an important differential for late onset disinhibition but runs an episodic course with elevated or irritable mood and reduced need for sleep, none of which are present. A steady two year decline without mood elevation does not fit. (Source: RANZCP: Dementia)

options.text: Provide a report to the court attributing the offence to stress following his resignation from employment
options.rationale: A report framing the offence as situational without investigating the underlying cause would mislead the court and deny him a diagnosis with major implications. The forensic opinion should follow the clinical assessment rather than precede it. (Source: RANZCP: Dementia)

options.text: Arrange neuroimaging with formal neuropsychological assessment and refer to a cognitive disorders service
options.rationale: Progressive disinhibition, loss of empathy, dietary change with carbohydrate craving, compulsive rituals and absent insight in late middle age, with preserved memory and orientation but impaired fluency and set shifting, is the behavioural variant frontotemporal syndrome. Structural and functional imaging with formal neuropsychological testing is what establishes it, and a normal bedside screen is expected and must not be taken as reassurance. (Source: RANZCP: Dementia)

options.text: Diagnose kleptomania and refer for cognitive behavioural therapy targeting the impulse to steal items
options.rationale: Kleptomania involves rising tension before the theft and relief afterwards, with items that are not needed and a person who recognises the behaviour as wrong. He took what he wanted openly and without concern, and the theft sits within a broader two year change in personality. (Source: RANZCP: Dementia)

options.text: Start an antidepressant for a late onset depressive episode presenting with apathy and social withdrawal
options.rationale: Late onset depression is a genuine mimic and often coexists, but he describes no low mood and his presentation is disinhibited and facetious rather than withdrawn. Serotonergic agents may help specific behaviours later but do not substitute for making the diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP: Dementia)

explanation.summary: Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia typically presents between the ages of forty five and sixty five with early and progressive change in personality and social conduct, including disinhibition, loss of empathy, apathy, compulsive and ritualistic behaviours, and hyperorality with a marked preference for sweet foods. Memory and orientation are relatively preserved early, so bedside cognitive screens are frequently normal and provide false reassurance, while executive deficits such as reduced verbal fluency and impaired set shifting are apparent on more detailed testing. Absent insight is close to universal and means the history must come from family. New criminal behaviour in middle age, particularly theft and socially inappropriate conduct in a person with no previous history, is a recognised presentation and carries substantial forensic consequences if the diagnosis is missed. Assessment requires structural and often functional neuroimaging, formal neuropsychological testing and specialist referral, with genetic counselling considered because a significant proportion of cases are familial.
key_points: Onset is typically between forty five and sixty five with personality change preceding memory loss
A normal bedside cognitive screen is expected and is not reassuring
Reduced verbal fluency and impaired set shifting reveal the executive deficit
Absent insight means collateral history from family is essential
New offending in middle age without prior history warrants cognitive assessment
explanation.pearls: Ask the family specifically about a new sweet tooth and about rigid daily routines, because hyperorality with carbohydrate preference and compulsive ritualistic behaviour are among the most discriminating early features and are almost never volunteered as medical symptoms, being reported instead as the person simply having become difficult.

subtopic_detail: Late onset depression with executive slowing and extensive white matter change on imaging
stem:
You are the old age psychiatry registrar reviewing a 74 year old man with his first depressive episode, beginning eighteen months ago. He has been treated with sertraline titrated to 200 mg daily for four months and then mirtazapine 45 mg nightly for a further four months, with minimal change.

His wife describes him as slowed rather than sad, sitting for hours without starting anything and needing to be prompted through each step of dressing. He denies pervasive guilt or worthlessness and says he simply cannot get going. He has hypertension, type 2 diabetes and a previous transient ischaemic attack, and his blood pressure has averaged 158/92 mmHg on home readings. He has no gait disturbance beyond mild slowing and no urinary incontinence. Magnetic resonance imaging shows confluent periventricular and deep white matter hyperintensities with several lacunes in the basal ganglia, and neuropsychological testing shows prominent deficits in initiation, planning and processing speed with relatively preserved recognition memory.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, BP 158/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Psychomotor slowing with reduced spontaneous speech, affect flat but reactive, no psychotic features, no focal weakness, mildly slowed gait with normal base, no incontinence
data_table.Investigations: Glycated haemoglobin 7.8 percent (less than 7.0 on treatment), low density lipoprotein cholesterol 3.2 mmol/L (less than 2.0 for secondary prevention), thyroid stimulating hormone 2.4 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), vitamin B12 340 pmol/L (150-700), magnetic resonance imaging showing confluent white matter hyperintensities with basal ganglia lacunes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence a cholinesterase inhibitor on the basis that the presentation reflects an emerging dementia syndrome
options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibitors are licensed for Alzheimer disease and dementia with Lewy bodies and have not shown benefit in pure vascular cognitive impairment. His memory is relatively preserved and the deficit is executive, so the drug target does not match. (Source: RANZCP: Dementia)

options.text: Refer for electroconvulsive therapy now given failure of two adequate trials of antidepressant medication
options.rationale: Electroconvulsive therapy is effective in older people and is the right answer for severe, psychotic, catatonic or life threatening depression, and it remains an option later. Proceeding to it before the vascular contribution and the behavioural deficit have been addressed skips reversible ground. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders)

options.text: Add low dose aripiprazole as augmentation and continue the current antidepressant at its present dose
options.rationale: Antipsychotic augmentation is an evidence based strategy in treatment resistant depression including in older adults, but it carries movement, metabolic and cerebrovascular risks in this population. It is a reasonable later step once vascular optimisation and behavioural treatment are in place. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Optimise his vascular risk factors alongside the psychiatric treatment and add a structured behavioural programme
options.rationale: Late onset depression with executive slowing, poor antidepressant response and confluent white matter disease is a vascular depression, in which cerebrovascular burden both contributes to the syndrome and predicts continued poor response to monotherapy escalation. Aggressive treatment of blood pressure, glycaemia and lipids addresses the substrate while a structured behavioural activation or problem solving programme compensates directly for the initiation deficit. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders)

options.text: Switch to a tricyclic antidepressant such as nortriptyline with therapeutic level monitoring during titration
options.rationale: Tricyclics remain effective in severe depression and levels can be monitored, but anticholinergic burden, orthostatic hypotension and falls make them a poor choice in a 74 year old with cerebrovascular disease. A third sequential monotherapy also ignores what the imaging and cognitive profile are indicating. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Vascular depression describes late onset depression occurring with significant cerebrovascular disease, characterised clinically by psychomotor slowing, apathy, prominent executive dysfunction and comparatively little guilt or self reproach. The imaging correlate is confluent deep and periventricular white matter hyperintensity with lacunes, reflecting disruption of frontostriatal circuits, and this burden predicts poorer and slower response to antidepressant monotherapy as well as higher relapse rates. Management is therefore broader than sequential drug switching and includes aggressive secondary prevention with blood pressure, glycaemic and lipid control, since progression of white matter disease worsens both mood and cognition. Psychological approaches that compensate directly for impaired initiation and planning, such as behavioural activation and problem solving therapy, have specific evidence in executive dysfunction and outperform insight oriented approaches. Electroconvulsive therapy and pharmacological augmentation remain available for those who do not respond to this combined approach.
key_points: Apathy and slowing with little guilt characterise the vascular depression phenotype
Confluent white matter change predicts poor antidepressant monotherapy response
Executive deficits with preserved recognition memory point to frontostriatal disruption
Vascular risk factor control is part of psychiatric management, not separate from it
Behavioural activation and problem solving therapy target the initiation deficit directly
explanation.pearls: Treat blood pressure of 158/92 mmHg in this man as a psychiatric intervention rather than a matter for his general practitioner alone, because progression of the white matter burden is what drives both the persistence of the mood disorder and the conversion to vascular cognitive impairment over the following years.

subtopic_detail: Adolescent unable to wake for school who sleeps normally on holidays and has failed antidepressant treatment
stem:
You are the child and adolescent psychiatry registrar seeing a 16 year old girl referred with school refusal and presumed depression. She has taken fluoxetine 20 mg each morning for five months without benefit and her general practitioner asks whether to increase it.

She cannot fall asleep before about 3 am no matter how early she goes to bed, and cannot be roused before 11 am on school days, arriving irritable, unfocused and falling asleep in class. During the summer holidays, when she went to bed at 3 am and woke at 11 am, she described herself as feeling completely well, energetic and sociable, with none of the low mood or fatigue seen in term time. She denies anhedonia outside the mornings, has close friendships, enjoys her art, and denies hopelessness or self harm. She has been prescribed melatonin 5 mg at 10 pm for the past two months, taken as instructed, with no change to her sleep onset time.

data_table.Examination: Alert and engaged during a 4 pm appointment, reactive affect, no psychomotor retardation, no psychotic features, no self harm marks
data_table.Investigations: Two week sleep diary and actigraphy showing sleep onset between 2:40 am and 3:20 am with wake between 10:50 am and 11:30 am on free days, total sleep time 8 hours on free days and 4.5 hours on school days, thyroid function and ferritin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase fluoxetine to 40 mg daily and review the response to the higher dose after a further six weeks
options.rationale: Dose escalation assumes a partially treated depressive episode, but full wellbeing on holidays with preserved friendships, interest and reactive affect is incompatible with a five month depressive episode. Continuing to treat the wrong diagnosis also carries the risk of activation and worsening insomnia. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders)

options.text: Increase the melatonin dose to 10 mg at the same time each night and continue for a further two months
options.rationale: Raising the dose while keeping the timing wrong produces a hypnotic and soporific effect rather than a phase shift, since the size of the circadian advance depends on when the dose is given relative to endogenous melatonin onset and not on how much is taken. Larger doses can also spill over into the following morning and worsen sleep inertia. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Delayed sleep phase)
source_refs: Sleep Health Foundation: Delayed sleep phase

options.text: Refer for a family based intervention addressing school refusal with a graded return to attendance plan
options.rationale: Graded return programmes are effective for anxiety driven school refusal, where the child can wake but cannot face attending. This girl cannot be roused at all and functions well once awake, so an attendance programme built on an anxiety model will fail against a biological phase delay. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders)

options.text: Prescribe a sedating antihistamine at bedtime to bring her sleep onset forward to a more conventional hour
options.rationale: Sedation can force sleep onset earlier for a night or two but does not move the underlying circadian phase, so the drug must be continued indefinitely while morning waking remains as difficult as before. Anticholinergic effects and next day sedation compound the school day impairment. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Move the melatonin to several hours before her current sleep onset and add timed morning bright light
options.rationale: Her sleep is normal in duration and quality when she is free to choose her timing, and the symptoms appear only when the schedule conflicts with her delayed phase, which identifies a circadian rhythm disorder rather than depression. Melatonin acts as a chronobiotic only when given roughly four to six hours before habitual sleep onset, so a dose at 10 pm falls far too close to a 3 am onset to shift anything, and pairing correctly timed low dose melatonin with bright light after waking advances the phase from both ends. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Delayed sleep phase)
source_refs: Sleep Health Foundation: Delayed sleep phase

explanation.summary: Delayed sleep wake phase disorder is the commonest circadian rhythm disorder of adolescence and is frequently misdiagnosed as depression or school refusal, because the daytime consequences of chronic sleep restriction closely resemble a depressive syndrome. The discriminating feature is that sleep is normal in duration, quality and refreshment when the person is free to choose their own timing, so wellbeing during holidays with an unchanged late schedule effectively excludes a primary mood disorder. A sleep diary with actigraphy over at least a week documents the pattern and is the practical diagnostic tool. The critical treatment principle is that melatonin behaves as a chronobiotic only when given several hours before habitual sleep onset, so a conventional bedtime dose in a markedly delayed adolescent acts as a mild hypnotic and produces no phase shift, which is exactly why the earlier prescription failed. Effective management combines low dose melatonin timed to the individual phase with bright light exposure after waking, avoidance of evening light, and a consistent wake time including at weekends, with the wake time being the single most important anchor.
key_points: Normal restorative sleep on a free schedule separates circadian delay from depression
Sleep diary with actigraphy over at least a week documents the phase
Melatonin shifts phase only when given hours before habitual sleep onset
Larger melatonin doses at the wrong time sedate rather than advance the rhythm
Morning bright light plus a fixed wake time anchors the advance most powerfully
explanation.pearls: Hold the wake time constant on weekends during treatment, because a single sleep in of two or three hours on a Saturday and Sunday re delays the phase by more than the week of timed melatonin and morning light has advanced it, and this is the commonest reason an otherwise correct treatment plan fails in adolescents.

sources.label: Sleep Health Foundation: Delayed sleep phase
